title: The Quotient Rule
summary: How to differentiate a fraction of two functions, with examples and a comparison with rewriting as powers.

p: If y = u/v, then dy/dx = [v (du/dx) − u (dv/dx)] / v². In words: (bottom × derivative of top − top × derivative of bottom) ÷ bottom squared. The order matters because of the minus sign.
If the denominator is a single term, divide first. y = (2x² + 3)/x = 2x + 3x⁻¹, so dy/dx = 2 − 3/x². This is quicker and safer than the quotient rule.

o: divide first and use the power rule

title: The Chain Rule
summary: How to differentiate a function of a function, with examples and combined use of the chain, product and quotient rules.

p: If y = f(u) and u = g(x), then dy/dx = (dy/du) × (du/dx). Think of an outer function and an inner function: differentiate the outside (leaving the inside alone) and multiply by the derivative of the inside.
1. y = (3x + 2)⁵. Let u = 3x + 2; then y = u⁵. dy/du = 5u⁴ and du/dx = 3. dy/dx = 15(3x + 2)⁴.
2. y = (x² + 1)³. Let u = x² + 1. dy/dx = 3u² × 2x = 6x(x² + 1)².
Product and chain: y = x(2x + 1)³. dy/dx = (2x + 1)³ + x × 6(2x + 1)² = (2x + 1)²(8x + 1).
Quotient and chain: y = (x² + 1)³/x. Write it with the quotient rule, using the chain rule for the top: dy/dx = [x × 6x(x² + 1)² − (x² + 1)³]/x² = (x² + 1)²(6x² − x² − 1)/x² = (x² + 1)²(5x² − 1)/x².

The chain rule links rates that depend on each other. If a circle's radius grows at 0.5 cm/s, how fast does the area grow when r = 10 cm? A = πr², so dA/dr = 2πr. dA/dt = dA/dr × dr/dt = 2π(10)(0.5) = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm²/s.

title: Rates of Change, Velocity and Acceleration
summary: Using derivatives to find velocity and acceleration of a moving body, and other rates of change.

p: If s is the displacement (distance from a fixed point) at time t, then the velocity is v = ds/dt and the acceleration is a = dv/dt = d²s/dt². A negative velocity means the body is moving in the negative direction.
A particle's position is s = t² + 4t (metres, seconds). v = 2t + 4. At t = 3, v = 10 m/s. a = 2 m/s² (constant).

(a) The body is at rest when v = 0: t = 1 s or t = 5 s. (b) At t = 1: s = 1 − 9 + 15 = 7 m. At t = 5: s = 125 − 225 + 75 = −25 m. (c) The acceleration is zero when 6t − 18 = 0, t = 3 s, when v = 27 − 54 + 15 = −12 m/s.
Volume of a sphere V = (4/3)πr³. dV/dr = 4πr². If the radius grows at 2 cm/s when r = 5 cm, then dV/dt = 4π(25)(2) = 200π ≈ 628 cm³/s.
Business: if the cost of making x items is C = 0.5x² + 10x + 200 (₦), the marginal cost is dC/dx = x + 10. At x = 8 the marginal cost is ₦18 per extra item.

title: Maximum and Minimum Values and Optimisation
summary: Finding turning points where dy/dx = 0, deciding whether they are maxima or minima, and solving practical optimisation problems.

p: At a maximum or minimum of a smooth curve, the tangent is horizontal, so dy/dx = 0. Such a point is a stationary (turning) point. To decide which kind: use the second derivative. If d²y/dx² > 0 the point is a minimum. If d²y/dx² < 0 it is a maximum.
y = x² − 2x − 3. dy/dx = 2x − 2 = 0, so x = 1. d²y/dx² = 2 > 0, so a minimum. y = 1 − 2 − 3 = −4. The minimum point is (1, −4). This agrees with the graph drawn earlier.

img.alt: The parabola y = x squared minus 2x minus 3 with its minimum point at (1, -4)
img.cap: The minimum of y = x² − 2x − 3 is at (1, −4).

p: y = x³ − 3x. dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0, so x = 1 or x = −1. d²y/dx² = 6x. At x = 1 it is 6 > 0: a minimum, y = −2. At x = −1 it is −6 < 0: a maximum, y = 2.
y = −x² + 4x + 1. dy/dx = −2x + 4 = 0, so x = 2. d²y/dx² = −2 < 0: a maximum, y = −4 + 8 + 1 = 5.

1. A farmer has 60 m of fencing for three sides of a rectangular pen (the fourth side is a wall). Let the two equal sides be x. The other side is 60 − 2x. Area A = x(60 − 2x) = 60x − 2x². dA/dx = 60 − 4x = 0, so x = 15. d²A/dx² = −4: a maximum. The sides are 15 m and 30 m and the area is 450 m².

2. A square sheet of card 12 cm by 12 cm has a square of side x cut from each corner and the sides are folded up to make an open box. V = x(12 − 2x)². dV/dx = (12 − 2x)(12 − 6x) = 0, so x = 2 (x = 6 is not possible). V = 2 × 8² = 128 cm³.

title: Integration: The Reverse of Differentiation
summary: Integration as the reverse of differentiation, the power rule for integration, and the constant of integration.

p: Integration is the reverse of differentiation. If d/dx (x³) = 3x², then ∫ 3x² dx = x³ + C. The integral sign ∫ means 'integrate', dx shows the variable and C is the constant of integration. We need C because the derivative of any constant is 0, so many functions (x³, x³ + 5, x³ − 2) have the same derivative.
Power rule: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1. In words: add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power.
Constant multiple: ∫ k f(x) dx = k ∫ f(x) dx. Sum and difference: ∫ (f ± g) dx = ∫ f dx ± ∫ g dx. Constants: ∫ k dx = kx + C.
∫ 4x³ dx = x⁴ + C.
∫ (x² + 2x) dx = x³/3 + x² + C.
Check any integral by differentiating the answer: d/dx [(2/3)x³ − (5/2)x² + 3x] = 2x² − 5x + 3 ✓.
The power rule does not work for n = −1. ∫ (1/x) dx = ln |x| + C (natural logarithm), which you will meet in further study.

title: Initial Conditions and Definite Integrals
summary: Finding the constant of integration from given information, and evaluating definite integrals between limits.

p: If we know a point on the curve (or a starting value), we can find C. Example: dy/dx = 6x − 2 and y = 5 when x = 1. y = 3x² − 2x + C. 5 = 3 − 2 + C, so C = 4. y = 3x² − 2x + 4.
Marginal cost: MC = 5x + 10 and the fixed cost is ₦200. C(x) = 2.5x² + 10x + C₀, and C(0) = 200, so C₀ = 200. The total cost of 8 units = 2.5(64) + 80 + 200 = 160 + 80 + 200 = ₦440.
Velocity: v = 3t² + 2 with s = 0 at t = 0 gives s = t³ + 2t.
∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f. No constant C is needed, because it cancels.
Examples. ∫₁⁴ x² dx = [x³/3]₁⁴ = 64/3 − 1/3 = 21. ∫₀² (x² + 2x) dx = [x³/3 + x²]₀² = 8/3 + 4 = 20/3. ∫₋₁² 3x² dx = [x³]₋₁² = 8 − (−1) = 9.
∫ₐᵇ f dx = −∫ᵇₐ f dx (reversing the limits changes the sign). ∫ₐᵃ f dx = 0. ∫ₐᵇ f dx + ∫ᵇᶜ f dx = ∫ₐᶜ f dx. ∫ₐᵇ k f dx = k ∫ₐᵇ f dx.
The distance moved between t = a and t = b is ∫ₐᵇ v dt. If v = 3t² + 2, the distance in the first 4 seconds is [t³ + 2t]₀⁴ = 64 + 8 = 72 m.

title: Area Under a Curve and Integration by Substitution
summary: Using definite integrals to find areas under curves and between curves, and the method of substitution for functions of a function.

p: The area between the curve y = f(x), the x-axis and the lines x = a and x = b is ∫ₐᵇ y dx, provided the curve is above the x-axis.
Example 1. The area under y = x² from x = 0 to x = 3 is ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3]₀³ = 9 square units.
Example 2. The area under y = 2x + 1 from x = 0 to x = 3 is [x² + x]₀³ = 12. (Check: a trapezium with parallel sides 1 and 7 and width 3 has area ½(1 + 7) × 3 = 12.)

img.alt: The curve y = x squared from x = 0 to x = 3 with the area under it shaded
img.cap: The shaded area is ∫₀³ x² dx = 9.

p: Area = ∫ (upper curve − lower curve) dx. The curves y = x and y = x² meet where x = x², at x = 0 and x = 1. Between them, y = x is above. Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.

The integral is negative where the curve is below the axis, but the area is positive. ∫₀³ (x² − 3x) dx = [x³/3 − 3x²/2]₀³ = 9 − 13.5 = −4.5. The area is 4.5 square units. If the curve crosses the axis, find each part separately.
For a function of a function, let u = the inner function. Example: ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁴ dx. Let u = x² + 1, so du = 2x dx. The integral becomes ∫ u⁴ du = u⁵/5 + C = (x² + 1)⁵/5 + C.
∫ (2x + 3)⁴ dx: u = 2x + 3, du = 2 dx, so dx = du/2. ∫ u⁴ du/2 = u⁵/10 + C = (2x + 3)⁵/10 + C.
∫ x(x² + 4)³ dx: u = x² + 4, du = 2x dx. ∫ (1/2) u³ du = u⁴/8 + C = (x² + 4)⁴/8 + C.

title: Functions and Mapping
summary: The meaning of a function, domain, codomain and range, and mapping diagrams.

p: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. We write f(x) = 2x + 3, or f: x → 2x + 3. The set of allowed inputs is the domain. The set in which the outputs lie is the codomain. The set of actual outputs is the range, which is part of the codomain.

A mapping diagram shows the domain and codomain as two ovals, with arrows from each input to its output. In the left diagram below, f(x) = 2x maps {1, 2, 3} into {2, 4, 6, 8}. The range is {2, 4, 6}; the element 8 in the codomain is not an output. In the right diagram, g(x) = x² maps {−2, 2, 1} into {4, 1}: two different inputs, −2 and 2, give the same output 4.

img.alt: Two mapping diagrams: f of x equals 2x as a one-to-one mapping, and g of x equals x squared as a many-to-one mapping
img.cap: A one-to-one and a many-to-one mapping.

p: Some functions cannot accept every number. f(x) = 1/(x − 2) is not defined at x = 2 (division by zero), so the domain is all real numbers except 2. g(x) = √(x − 1) needs x − 1 ≥ 0, so the domain is x ≥ 1.
Think of f as a machine: put in x, apply the rule, and take out f(x). Example: f(x) = x² − 3x. f(5) = 25 − 15 = 10. If f(x) = 10, then x² − 3x − 10 = 0, (x − 5)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 5 or x = −2.

title: Types of Functions, Composite and Inverse Functions
summary: One-to-one, onto, many-to-one and bijective functions, composite functions and inverse functions.

p: One-to-one (injective): different inputs give different outputs. f(x) = 2x is one-to-one. Onto (surjective): every element of the codomain is an output, so the range equals the codomain. One-to-one and onto (bijective): a perfect pairing of inputs and outputs. Many-to-one: different inputs can give the same output. g(x) = x² is many-to-one because g(2) = g(−2) = 4.
The composite function fg means 'do g first, then f': fg(x) = f(g(x)).
Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x². fg(x) = f(x²) = 2x² + 3. gf(x) = g(2x + 3) = (2x + 3)² = 4x² + 12x + 9. Notice that fg ≠ gf in general. For x = 2: fg(2) = 11 and gf(2) = 49.
The inverse function f⁻¹ undoes f. Only a one-to-one function has an inverse. To find it: write y = f(x); make x the subject; then swap x and y.
Example 1. f(x) = 2x + 3. y = 2x + 3, so x = (y − 3)/2. f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Check: f(1) = 5 and f⁻¹(5) = 1.
The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.

p: Power rule: d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹. Product: (uv)′ = u v′ + v u′. Quotient: (u/v)′ = (v u′ − u v′)/v². Chain: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. Turning points: dy/dx = 0; check with d²y/dx². Tangent: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). Normal: gradient −1/m.
